tldr: By imitating computationally heavy nonlinear time-optimal MPC (TOMPC) with a neural network and using an integrated framework featuring self-informed sampling (SIFS)—which queries only the states that truly need labels using a learned time-to-go (T2G)—this work achieves ultra-fast 1 kHz swing-up control on real hardware with less than half the data and roughly one-third of the training time.
overview:
Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) is an extremely powerful control method. It pushes system and actuator constraints to their limits to reach a target state in the shortest possible time. However, solving the underlying nonconvex optimization problem demands immense computational effort. This makes real-time execution virtually impossible and turns data generation for supervised learning into a massive bottleneck.

To overcome this, the authors built an integrated practical pipeline for neural network imitation of TOMPC (NNMPC). The key idea is self-informed sampling (SIFS). The network simultaneously predicts both the control input and the remaining time to reach the goal (time-to-go: T2G). By monitoring this T2G trajectory, the system self-detects the exact moments the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior and queries the expert. In addition, the framework bundles solutions for real-world issues: mitigating dataset correlation, weighting local minima (competing labels) caused by nonconvexity, enforcing constraints via safety filters, and compensating for model mismatch using auxiliary controllers.

In experiments on a Furuta pendulum (rotary inverted pendulum), the proposed method matched or exceeded the performance of standard DAgger and MC-dropout while requiring less than half the training data and roughly one-third of the training time. It boosted the control frequency from the original MPC's ~1.36 Hz up to 1 kHz via GPU inference (deployed at 250 Hz on the physical setup), successfully achieving time-optimal swing-up and stabilization on real hardware just as in simulation.
contributions: Proposed SIFS, a highly data-efficient sampling strategy that monitors the decreasing trend of learned time-to-go (T2G) to pinpoint states where the policy fails and query the expert only there.

Constructed a comprehensive, integrated NNMPC architecture that simultaneously tackles dataset correlation, competing labels from nonconvex MPC, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction, and model mismatch.

Established a lightweight sample-weighting scheme based on comparing T2G values among neighboring samples, reducing the negative impact of local minima and suboptimal labels without requiring an additional network.

Demonstrated on real Furuta pendulum hardware that the control frequency can be raised from 1.4 Hz to up to 1 kHz (250 Hz on hardware) while preserving a region of attraction (ROA) comparable to the expert TOMPC.

sections.heading: The Barriers to Neural Time-Optimal MPC and How to Tackle Them
sections.summary: TOMPC can push fast nonlinear systems to their physical limits, but its heavy online compute prevents real-world deployment. Neural imitation is a promising alternative, yet bang-bang behavior, hard terminal constraints, and costly data generation remain severe bottlenecks.
sections.details:
Model predictive control (MPC) is a powerful framework that handles constraints explicitly. However, when applying time-optimal MPC (TOMPC)—which drives a system to its target in minimum time—to fast dynamical systems, computation time far exceeds typical sampling intervals. To break this barrier, researchers increasingly use neural network imitation via behavioral cloning (NNMPC), training a network on offline MPC solutions to enable ultra-fast real-time inference.

Yet existing NNMPC research has critical gaps. Most prior work focuses on tracking quadratic costs in simulation. Nonconvex TOMPC with long horizons and hard terminal constraints poses three major challenges:

- The expert MPC itself is so computationally demanding that generating training data becomes the bottleneck.
- Time-optimal control naturally leads to bang-bang behavior (inputs saturating at upper and lower bounds), requiring dense data around switching points.
- Issues like dataset correlation, covariate shift, competing local minima, constraint violations, and model mismatch have only been studied in isolation, lacking an integrated system design.

This is where this work steps in. The authors designed an integrated architecture addressing all these hurdles simultaneously, introduced the data-efficient SIFS sampling strategy, and proved its viability through hardware experiments.

sections.heading: Where Did Prior Methods Fall Short?
sections.summary: Previous works treated dataset correlation, multimodal solutions, active learning sample efficiency, constraint satisfaction, and adaptability separately. However, existing active learning metrics—like epistemic uncertainty or trajectory divergence—fail as reliable proxies for control failure.
sections.details:
Explicit MPC uses lookup tables to speed up execution, but it breaks down in higher dimensions. Learning continuous mappings with neural networks is attractive, but prior work leaves key issues unsolved:

### Dataset Correlation and Competing Labels
Time-series data from MPC violates the i.i.d. assumption and tends to cluster in specific regions. Furthermore, nonconvex optimization yields competing labels: different local minima from the exact same state (e.g., swinging the pendulum clockwise vs. counter-clockwise). Training with standard mean squared error (MSE) averages these solutions, producing an invalid intermediate control input that tracks neither mode.

### Sample Efficiency and Limits of Active Learning
DAgger is the standard approach to combat covariate shift (distribution shift between training and execution). However, it queries the expert indiscriminately, even in states where the current policy already performs well. For computationally intensive TOMPC, this is simply too slow. Methods targeting epistemic uncertainty (like MC-dropout) or trajectory divergence (like STRIDE) have been proposed to focus queries.

Yet they suffer from three fundamental flaws: first, high uncertainty does not necessarily mean control failure, leading to overconfidence or false alarms. Second, they ignore the system's sensitivity to control errors. Third, they do not account for how errors propagate through the dynamics. They cannot distinguish between errors that self-correct in the next step and those that trigger immediate divergence.

### Constraint Satisfaction and Model Adaptation
Vanilla neural networks cannot guarantee state or input constraints. While penalty terms in loss functions or control barrier functions (CBFs) are common, methods that require learning dual variables complicate data generation further. Additionally, the inability to adapt to real-world model mismatch without retraining has been a major roadblock to hardware deployment.

sections.heading: An Integrated Architecture for Efficient Learning and Control Using T2G
sections.summary: The proposed framework combines optimal dataset subsampling, T2G-based loss weighting, and SIFS active learning that spots control failures via T2G trends. For hardware deployment, it adds a safety filter and lightweight auxiliary controllers.
sections.details:
Here is how the proposed pipeline works and how each component is designed:

### III-A Expert TOMPC
To steer the system to the target state in minimum time, the expert uses a nonconvex MPC with an exponentially weighted objective and hard terminal constraints. Here, Time-to-Go (T2G)—the time corresponding to the number of predicted steps required to reach within a tolerance $\xi$ of the target—is defined and treated as a value function.

### III-B & III-C Dataset Subsampling and T2G-Based Weighting
To eliminate redundancy from temporal correlation, the authors use an Optimally-Sampled Dataset algorithm from prior work, pruning data while preserving information density. To address competing labels from nonconvexity, each sample $\mathbf{x}_i$ has its T2G compared against the distance-weighted average $\overline{\mathrm{T2G}}$ of its $M$ nearest neighbors. Trajectories closer to the true minimum time receive higher training weights $w_{\mathrm{knn}}$. This lightweight weighting avoids training an extra discriminator network.

### III-D Self-Informed Sampling (SIFS)
This is the core insight of the paper. The network predicts both the control input and the T2G. Along a truly time-optimal trajectory, the T2G must decrease by exactly one sampling interval ($\Delta t$) at every step.

Because the network predicts T2G purely from the current state without subtracting past values, maintaining this linear downward trend by chance is virtually impossible unless control is accurate and the network genuinely understands T2G. During rollouts, the framework tracks predicted T2G trends. If T2G stops decreasing or stalls, the system flags that the policy has diverged from time-optimal behavior. By prioritizing queries to the expert around the states just before the flag and during early trajectory phases, it selectively collects only the data that truly needs reinforcement.

### III-E & III-F Controller Adaptability and Constraint Guarantees
To compensate for real-world model mismatch, the authors introduce lightweight auxiliary controllers that require no retraining. They examine two variants: a dynamic inversion compensator (DIC), which reproduces nominal output derivatives on an estimated real-system model, and an LQR that feeds back residuals relative to predicted states. To prevent constraint violations, they combine log-barrier and quadratic penalties during training with a differentiable safety filter in the output layer that projects controls to ensure strict constraint satisfaction.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup on the Demanding Furuta Pendulum
sections.summary: The authors chose the highly nonlinear, underactuated Furuta pendulum for a minimum-time swing-up task from the downward position. They trained a 3-layer, 512-neuron MLP using an iterative SIFS loop.
sections.details:
To validate the method, the authors selected the classic yet challenging Furuta pendulum as their benchmark.

### IV-A Pendulum and Expert Setup
The state vector consists of arm and pendulum angles and velocities, $\mathbf{x}=(\theta_1, \theta_2, \dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2)$, and the input is base angular acceleration $u=\ddot{\theta}_1$. The horizon is $N=60$ steps ($\Delta t = 0.03$ s, 1.8 s lookahead), discretized using Runge-Kutta 4th order (RK4). The task is a demanding TOMPC problem: swing up and stabilize the pendulum from hanging downward to fully upright within a single horizon while respecting base angle and input limits. Solutions were generated using the Impact library and the Fatrop solver, warm-started from a KD-tree database of past feasible solutions.

### IV-B & IV-C Network Architecture and Training Loop
The network is an MLP with 3 hidden layers of 512 nodes each and $\tanh$ activations. It takes an 8-dimensional input (current state and target state) and outputs two values: the control input and the T2G.

Training proceeds in two stages:
- Pre-training on an initial grid dataset of 15,601 points (1,200 epochs, learning rate $8\times 10^{-4}$).
- Iterative training with SIFS over 1,441 iterations. This generated 1,189,320 expert points in total, compressed to 708,312 points via optimal sampling for training (minibatch size 4,096, 70 epochs per iteration, learning rate $10^{-6}$).

sections.heading: Simulation Results: Matching and Occasionally Outperforming the Expert
sections.summary: Across 1,000 random initial states, NNMPC matched the expert MPC's 95.7% success rate. Inference time dropped to under 1 ms on a GPU, enabling a 1 kHz control frequency—over 700 times faster than the original ~1.4 Hz MPC.
sections.details:
In simulation, the authors compared the closed-loop performance of the expert MPC and NNMPC across 1,000 randomly sampled initial states over a 3.6-second duration.

### Convergence and Time-to-Target
Both controllers successfully converged to the target in 91.5% of cases. NNMPC succeeded alone in 4.2% of cases, while the expert MPC succeeded alone in 4.3%. Their effective regions of attraction are virtually identical.

The median time to reach the goal was 1.35 s for the expert MPC and 1.62 s for NNMPC, showing only a slight delay for the imitation policy. Remarkably, NNMPC reached the target faster than the expert MPC in several instances (Fig. F3b). This suggests that while the nonconvex MPC got trapped in local optima, NNMPC generalized across many trajectories and discovered globally superior behavior.

### Massive Reduction in Compute Time
The difference in control frequency was stark. The original TOMPC required significant optimization time, running reliably at only around 1.36 Hz (~735 ms period). In contrast, NNMPC achieved roughly 100 Hz on a CPU (Intel Core i7) and consistently stayed below 1 ms per inference on a mobile GPU (Nvidia Quadro P1000), making ultra-fast control loops up to 1 kHz fully feasible.

captions.F3: Distribution of time-to-target across 1,000 initial states (left) and their pairwise difference (right). NNMPC closely approaches MPC with a median of 1.62 s vs. 1.35 s, and the right-hand distribution shows cases where the difference is negative (NNMPC reaches the goal faster).

sections.heading: Ablation Study: Do the Proposed Components Really Help?
sections.summary: Ablations show that T2G-based weighting substantially cuts failure rates, while SIFS matches DAgger performance with half the data in one-third the time. Auxiliary controllers also provide strong robustness across wide parameter variations.
sections.details:
The authors conducted detailed ablation experiments to analyze the individual impact of each pipeline component.

### VI-A Effect of Competing Label Weighting
Disabling T2G-based sample weighting clearly increased the failure rate (the percentage of runs failing to reach the target within 3.6 seconds). Downweighting inferior solutions relative to neighboring trajectories effectively prevents multimodal policies from collapsing.

### VI-B Data Efficiency and Training Time of SIFS
The authors compared SIFS against standard uniform sampling (DAgger) and epistemic uncertainty sampling via MC-dropout (20 forward passes, 30% dropout rate). SIFS reduced failure rates much faster, converging with less than half the training data and roughly one-third of the training time required by DAgger or MC-dropout. This validates the advantage of evaluating the multi-step T2G trend rather than single-state uncertainty.

### VI-C Robustness to Model Mismatch via Auxiliary Controllers
The setup was evaluated under systematic model parameter perturbations of up to $\pm 100\%$, including pendulum mass $m_2$, link length $L_1$, and viscous friction $b_2$ (Fig. F6). Vanilla NNMPC saw its success rate plummet with small shifts. However, pairing it with auxiliary controllers like DIC or LQR preserved high success rates without any retraining.

captions.F6: Success rate heatmaps under systematic model parameter variations. Compared to vanilla NNMPC (left), adding DIC (center) or LQR (right) dramatically improves resilience against modeling errors.

sections.heading: Real Hardware Swing-Up on the Furuta Pendulum
sections.summary: The proposed NNMPC was deployed on physical hardware, successfully achieving swing-up and stabilization from a hanging position in a 250 Hz control loop. Trajectories matched simulation closely, proving reliable real-world control.
sections.details:
Trained in simulation, the NNMPC was deployed onto a physical Furuta pendulum testbed.

### Hardware Setup and Implementation
The base is driven by a stepper motor, and pendulum angles are measured by an incremental encoder with 4,096 pulses per revolution. Over EtherCAT communication (using the SOEM library), the I/O thread ran at 1 kHz while the NNMPC inference and control thread ran at 250 Hz. The entire pipeline ran in real time on a standard Linux laptop with a mobile GPU.

### Swing-Up Results and Observations
Starting from the hanging position, NNMPC smoothly built momentum, swung the pendulum up, and stabilized it upright (Fig. F8). Real-world state trajectories matched simulation results very closely.

The only noticeable difference was minor high-frequency chattering in control inputs near the upright equilibrium. This was caused by sensor noise and minor residual model mismatch. It did not compromise system stability, and the authors note that it can be easily smoothed out with a low-pass filter on the NNMPC output.

captions.F8: Photo sequence of time-optimal swing-up and stabilization on the physical Furuta pendulum. The pendulum swings up dynamically from hanging (0.00s to 1.79s) and settles cleanly at the target upright position (2.20s).

sections.heading: Summary and Future Directions
sections.summary: This study presents an integrated framework for data-efficient, real-time neural imitation of nonlinear TOMPC, validated in both simulation and real-world hardware. Future work points toward mixture density networks for multimodality and continual learning.
sections.details:
This paper presented a complete integrated architecture to imitate nonlinear time-optimal MPC (TOMPC) with neural networks, overcoming computational bottlenecks that previously hindered real-time use.

Key takeaways include:
- SIFS leverages T2G to cut expert data generation by half and reduce training time to roughly one-third.
- T2G-based sample weighting effectively mitigates competing labels caused by nonconvex optimization.
- Worst-case computation time was reduced by over 700x (under 1 ms on a GPU), enabling 250 Hz time-optimal swing-up on physical hardware.

For future work, the authors highlight using Mixture Density Networks to fully represent multiple equally optimal modes (such as swinging left vs. right) and adopting continual learning to prevent training times from ballooning as datasets expand.

takeaways: Using the trajectory trend of a value function (T2G) as an active learning trigger directly detects control performance degradation, making it vastly more sample-efficient than output uncertainty or state-space distance metrics.
When learning from nonconvex MPC, weighting samples by comparing their cost against local neighbors is essential to prevent policy collapse caused by competing labels.

For neural imitation of heavy optimization, a hybrid setup—pairing the network with lightweight analytical compensators (DIC, LQR) and external safety filters—is the most practical path to real hardware deployment.
limitations: When multiple distinct paths are equally time-optimal (e.g., perfectly symmetric modes), sample weighting cannot pick a single winner, leaving potential ambiguity in the learned policy.
Near the upright equilibrium, sensitivity to sensor noise and model mismatch can cause high-frequency control chattering, requiring additional output filtering.
Because the dataset grows cumulatively across SIFS iterations, applying the framework to longer-horizon tasks will require continual learning approaches to prevent training times from scaling up.
